  1. TactileVLA-EdgeRobotics + ML, 2026 Imitation-learning policies for robot manipulation on a sub-$300 SO-101 arm, vision only. 18 of 20

    Teach a low-cost arm to pick up a deformable object by imitating human demonstration, then check it works in a part of the workspace it never practiced in.

    My part. I built the leader-follower rig, collected the 160 demonstrations, trained both policies, ran the hand-scored evaluation and patched LeRobot's recording code. Solo project.

    How it works

    1. Teleoperate. I move the leader arm by hand and the follower arm copies it, so every demonstration is a real motion of the robot.
    2. Collect. 20 demonstrations in each of the 8 outer cells of a 3x3 grid, sweeping 19 grasp orientations. The centre cell, B2, gets none.
    3. Train. An ACT policy, and a fine-tuned SmolVLA (450M), in LeRobot on one consumer GPU (an RTX 3060).
    4. Test. Deformable-object pick-and-place trials on the real arm with the leader disconnected, scored by hand, plus the never-seen cell B2.

    Results

    • ACT: 18 of 20 hand-scored pick-and-place trials on a deformable object
    • SmolVLA (450M, fine-tuned): 16 of 20 hand-scored trials
    • Both policies succeeded in B2, a cell held out of training
    • Dataset: 160 demonstrations, 67,693 frames
    • Hardware: an SO-101 leader-follower rig built for under $300
    • Submitted a patch to Hugging Face LeRobot (PR #3798) diagnosing a streaming-dataset collate crash on unconverted PIL images: 86 lines across 2 files with a regression test.
    • Patched LeRobot's recording and motor code (phase-aware controls, camera-stall tolerance, retries on dropped packets) so multi-hour recording sessions stayed stable.

  2. Zer0Sh0tRobotics, hackathon, 2026 A voice-controlled, low-cost robot arm that zero-shots new tasks: it turns spoken requests into pick, place and point actions with no task-specific demonstrations or retraining. 3rd Place, Best Overall

    Make a cheap arm do an arbitrary spoken task without collecting demonstrations or retraining for it.

    My part. I wrote the entire codebase end to end. The award and the demo are the team's. Team: Srijan Kumbam, Vishal Naveen, Siddharth Mohan, Hao Tran.

    How it works

    1. Hear. ElevenLabs transcribes the spoken request.
    2. Decide. A local command router handles common commands. Claude handles open-ended requests through tool calls (pick, place, point) that name object IDs and destination zones.
    3. See. Gemini Robotics-ER 2 Preview returns object labels and image locations. A local vision system links them to tracked objects using calibrated geometry, the prop catalog and AprilTags.
    4. Move. Calibrated coordinates and inverse kinematics turn each tool call into motion, with motion checks, behind a fail-closed safety runner.

    Results

    • 3rd Place, Best Overall at SwampHacks XII, out of 141 teams (team of 4)
    • No task-specific demonstrations or retraining: the task comes from the spoken request
    • Ran on my own SO-101 arm, the one I built for TactileVLA-Edge.

  3. Lucid DreamsVision, hackathon, 2026 A team of 4 built it: it turns a video or a few photos into a photoreal, life-size 3D person standing in your room, in Meta Quest passthrough, opened from one link in the Quest browser. Top 10 Finalist

    Put a photoreal, life-size 3D person in your room, from a video or a few photos, in a headset, with nothing to install.

    My part. Court Side, the animated-avatar pipeline and the GPU job scripts. Team: Ojasva Mishra, Atina Ruvinova, Ian Hoang, Vishal Naveen.

    How it works

    1. Views. 4DAnyone (SIGGRAPH Asia 2026) turns one clip into 48 synchronized views.
    2. Fit. Each person is fit as 4D Gaussians with gsplat on 12 NVIDIA B200 GPUs: 7,000 Adam steps for the first frame, then 1,500 per frame, about 285K Gaussians per frame.
    3. Use. Learn (lessons with follow-along markers), Play (chess against Fischer and Carlsen likenesses, tennis against a Federer likeness, shooting with LeBron), Court Side, and Talk (cloned-voice replies). Not affiliated with any of the people portrayed.

    Results

    • Top 10 Finalist at Gator Hack V (team of 4), built in one weekend on real footage
    • Replays reach 26.0-31.9 dB PSNR and 0.963-0.982 SSIM against the generated views (not real footage)
    • Phantom-limb fix: on the jump-shot clip, spill outside the person fell 2.3% to 0.4%; view PSNR rose 0.5-2.1 dB across the 5 re-done clips

  4. Sixth SenseiOS + on-device ML, 2023 An iOS navigation aid for blind and low-vision users: on-device obstacle detection, distance from a single camera, and spoken AR routes. 15 fps

    Help blind and low-vision users navigate by spotting obstacles in their path and telling them about them.

    My part. I built the app: Swift, ARKit and a YOLOv8n Core ML detector running entirely on the phone. Solo project.

    How it works

    1. Modeled obstacle distance with no depth sensor: monocular pinhole geometry over a 21-class reference-size table, Kalman-filtering the mean of width-, height- and area-derived estimates.
    2. Recorded indoor routes with 6-DoF ARKit tracking, with spoken turn-by-turn directions.
    3. Scoped accessibility requirements with the City of Tampa ADA coordinator.
    4. Voice commands (2024 demo build): the October 2024 demo build was voice-controlled (you start a route by saying it). That build's source wasn't kept, so the public repository has the spoken output but not the voice input.

    Results

    • 15 fps sustained detection on an iPhone 14 Pro (the app's frame cap)
    • 12.7 MB YOLOv8n Core ML model, running fully on device
    • 3rd place, 2024 Congressional App Challenge

Firmware Engineer Gator Motorsports, Formula SAE racing team, University of Florida

Aug 2026 - Present
Gainesville, FL

I built the car's real-time telemetry system in Rust: bare-metal firmware on a dual-core NXP microcontroller that streams live sensor data over 1 Gbps Ethernet to a multithreaded server.

  • Streams live sensor data at 10 Hz (every 100 ms) using under 0.001% of the link, with headroom for hundreds more signals.
  • Brought up a complete 3-layer networking stack: the Ethernet MAC driver, a PHY configured over MDIO, and an async IPv4/UDP stack (embassy-net), running as a background task.
  • The whole codec is no_std, so one shared implementation runs on both the microcontroller and the server, with no duplicated protocol logic.
  • Engineered a real-time telemetry system in Rust on an NXP i.MX RT1176 (1 GHz Arm Cortex-M7 + 400 MHz Cortex-M4) and a multithreaded server, linked over 1 Gbps Ethernet.
  • Moved the chip's temperature-sensor driver from blocking polling to interrupt-driven async (Embassy) so the CPU runs other tasks instead of busy-waiting.

Undergraduate Researcher TEA Lab, University of Florida, Trustworthy Engineered Autonomy Lab

Oct 2026 - Present
Gainesville, FL

Research on certified, uncertainty-aware 3D perception for self-driving cars: a framework that sorts every perception output into certified, budgeted or withheld trust levels, with statistical guarantees.

  • Trained 32 multi-task ResNet-18 perception models (4 output heads) on 342K Waymo Open Dataset training images, using ~120 NVIDIA B200 GPU-hours on a UF GPU cluster.
  • Ran a 27-configuration (3x3x3) factorial study of a 4-term multi-task loss, plus a 12-run one-factor sweep, comparing 41 configurations across 4 metrics. Reusing 7 already-trained models cut 27 runs to 20, saving ~26% of compute.
  • Cut validation position error (RMSE) by up to 8% over the baseline (5.87 to 5.40 m) while keeping failure detection on par. One run per setting on validation data; a multi-seed check is in progress.
  • Found that a higher error-head weight lowered RMSE in 7 of 9 controlled comparisons, a direction the one-factor sweep missed; the lab commissioned two follow-up runs.
  • Mapped the accuracy-reliability trade-off: failure-detection AUROC up to 0.87 and error-ranking correlation up 55% (Spearman 0.50 to 0.78), at a measured cost of up to 1.7 m RMSE. The detector matched but rarely beat the model's built-in uncertainty baseline (5 of 27 configs, by <= 0.005).
  • Ran training 3.5x in parallel with Slurm job arrays within the lab's shared 24-GPU limit, finishing a 73 GPU-hour grid in about 21 hours of wall-clock time.
  • Built an automated pipeline that generates 41-configuration comparison tables across 4 accuracy and reliability metrics straight from training logs, using validation data only, to protect the held-out calibration set behind the framework's statistical guarantees.
